title: Food tells the journey
hook: bagels, kubbeh, injera, shakshuka: the food follows the wanderings
carry: a map of everywhere we've been

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jewish humor, the two jesters in the market, and the line laugh. Did your gentle joke find the person who needed it? A new week starts in the kitchen. Day one thousand fifty-one.

Bagels. Kubbeh. Injera. Shakshuka. Say them out loud and you've crossed half a map. A ring of dough boiled and then baked. Dumplings of semolina or rice with meat folded inside, simmered in a sour soup. A soft, spongy flatbread for tearing and scooping. Eggs cooked in a pan of tomatoes and peppers. Each one sits on Jewish tables, and each one came from somewhere else, with someone. A family's food is a map of everywhere they've lived, and Jewish food tells that story plainly. Today's line: food tells the journey.
screen: `BAGELS, KUBBEH, INJERA, SHAKSHUKA.` → `HALF A MAP.` → `A FAMILY'S FOOD IS A MAP.`

segments.voice: The Torah already ties food to a journey. In Deuteronomy, a farmer brings the first fruits of the harvest in a basket and sets them down before the altar. He doesn't just hand them over. He has to tell a story, and it begins: "A wandering Aramean was my father." It goes on: down into Egypt, slavery, rescue, and finally this land and this fruit. The basket is the end of the journey; the words are the road that led there. The Haggadah later reads the same Hebrew another way, as an Aramean who tried to destroy our father, meaning Laban chasing Jacob. Two readings, one verse, and both of them a story told over food. The seder plate works the same way. Matzah, the bread of affliction. Bitter herbs. A meal you eat in order to remember a road. Then the laws of Shabbat shaped the stove itself. The Torah says: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." So Jewish cooks in lands far apart found a way to have a hot meal on Saturday without lighting a fire: a pot started before sundown on Friday, left to cook slowly through the night. Ashkenazi families call theirs cholent. Moroccan families make dafina. Sephardi families make hamin. Same law, different pots, depending on where the road went. And the dishes in today's hook trace those roads. Bagels from the Jewish bakeries of Eastern Europe. Kubbeh in the kitchens of Iraqi and Kurdish Jews. Injera on the tables of Beta Israel in Ethiopia. Shakshuka from North Africa. When families moved, they carried recipes the way the farmer carried his story. Today's line: food tells the journey.
screen: `A WANDERING ARAMEAN WAS MY FATHER.` · `A MEAL EATEN TO REMEMBER A ROAD.` · `NO FIRE ON SHABBAT, SO A SLOW POT.` · `RECIPES CARRIED LIKE A STORY.` · then, large: `FOOD TELLS THE JOURNEY.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: cook one dish with a story. You won't cook it right now. For now, sit and breathe, and go looking for the dish. Something a parent, a grandparent or a friend made, or something from a culture you love. Smell it in your memory. Hear the kitchen it came from. Then ask its story, the way the farmer had to tell his: where did this come from? Who carried it here? What changed along the way? Choose the day you'll cook it, and who you'll tell its story to while it's on the table. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for whoever carried it. The bell holds the time.
Cholent. The slow-cooked Shabbat stew Ashkenazi Jews started before sundown Friday, one of many names, dafina, hamin, for the same law of no fire on the Sabbath. Today's word.
Your line: a map of everywhere we've been. Today, at one meal, ask where one thing on the plate came from, and who brought it. Day one thousand fifty-one.

howItsDone: Jewish families keep dishes from the places their families have lived, cook slow Shabbat stews such as cholent, dafina and hamin that need no fire on Saturday, and tell the story of the Exodus over the foods of the Passover seder.
